chief_complaint: palpitations, hand tremors, weight loss of 6kg, and heat intolerance for 2 months
hpi_details: 28F reports racing heart beat (palpitations) even at rest, fine shaking of hands, feeling sweaty and hot in cool rooms, and 6kg weight loss over 2 months. Menstrual cycles have become light and irregular.
ideas: thinks she has severe anxiety or panic disorder
expectations: wants medication to stop the palpitations

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes confirming thyrotoxicosis with TSH and free T4/T3 and controlling symptoms with a beta-blocker while working up Graves' disease before starting definitive antithyroid therapy, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: palpitations, hand tremors, weight loss of 6kg, and heat intolerance for 2 months

Key HPI features: 28F reports racing heart beat (palpitations) even at rest, fine shaking of hands, feeling sweaty and hot in cool rooms, and 6kg weight loss over 2 months. Menstrual cycles have become light and irregular.
Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Hyperthyroidism, highly suggestive of Graves disease.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Anxiety/panic disorder without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Very high fever with extreme agitation — could herald thyroid storm.
management_principles: Assess pregnancy status before selecting antithyroid therapy, since methimazole carries teratogenic risk in the first trimester and propylthiouracil is preferred if treatment is needed during early pregnancy

Confirm thyrotoxicosis with TSH and free T4/T3, assess for Graves disease, and use a beta-blocker for symptomatic control; when antithyroid therapy is indicated, counsel on methimazole adverse effects and obtain baseline blood count and liver tests
Screen for eye involvement (Graves' orbitopathy) on exam and refer to Ophthalmology if present
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Hyperthyroidism, highly suggestive of Graves disease. palpitations, hand tremors, weight loss of 6kg, and heat intolerance for 2 months. 28F reports racing heart beat (palpitations) even at rest, fine shaking of hands, feeling sweaty and hot in cool rooms, and 6kg weight loss over 2 months. Menstrual cycles have become light and irregular.
reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Hyperthyroidism, highly suggestive of Graves disease.
reference_soap.assessment: Hyperthyroidism, highly suggestive of Graves' disease, given the resting tachycardia, tremor, weight loss despite normal appetite, heat intolerance, and menstrual irregularity in a young woman.
reference_soap.plan: Confirm thyrotoxicosis with TSH and free T4/T3 and assess for Graves disease with receptor antibodies and/or uptake imaging when appropriate. Use a beta-blocker for symptomatic control if no contraindication. When methimazole is indicated, obtain baseline blood count and liver tests and counsel the patient to stop it and seek urgent evaluation for fever, sore throat, jaundice, or dark urine. Assess pregnancy status and intentions before treatment selection. Refer to Endocrinology.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Hyperthyroidism, highly suggestive of Graves disease.
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for palpitations, hand tremors, weight loss of 6kg, and heat intolerance for 2 months
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for endocrinology
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies for Hyperthyroidism, highly suggestive of Graves disease.

teaching.one_liner: Excess thyroid hormone causing resting palpitations, tremor, weight loss despite normal eating, and heat intolerance in a young woman — treated with methimazole and a beta-blocker for symptom control.
red_flags: Very high fever with extreme agitation — could herald thyroid storm

must_ask.say: Does your heart race even when you're resting?
Have you noticed your hands shaking?
Have you lost weight without trying to diet?
Do you feel hot or sweaty in cool rooms?

history.answer: My hands have been shaking and my heart has been racing like crazy for the past two months.
The shaking is most noticeable when I hold my arms out, type, or hold a cup of water, but it feels like it is there all day.
It is in both of my hands equally. My head, legs, and voice haven't been shaking at all.
It started gradually about two months ago, and both the shaking and the heart racing have gotten steadily worse.
No, I haven't had any sudden numbness, weakness on one side, or trouble speaking.
It gets worse when I'm stressed or tired, and resting my hands doesn't completely stop the trembling.
It is really affecting my work as a web designer because typing and using the mouse are so hard, and I spill drinks from cups.
My handwriting has gotten very shaky and messy, but the letters aren't getting tiny or cramped.
No, I don't feel slow or stiff at all. If anything, I feel hyperactive and restless, like I can't sit still.
My smell is fine, and I haven't had constipation; actually, I have had two or three loose bowel movements every single day.
No, I have no problem with my balance and I haven't been stumbling or losing my footing.
My heart pounds and beats very fast even when I am just lying down and resting on the sofa.
I feel hot all the time and sweat constantly, even when the air conditioner is running and everyone else is chilly.
I lost 6 kilograms over the last two months without trying, even though my appetite has increased and I eat more.
I've been feeling extremely anxious and irritable, and I have a terrible time falling asleep at night.
No, the trembling doesn't happen just when I skip meals or feel hungry; it is there constantly.
I just have one regular cup of coffee in the morning, which has always been my normal routine.
I only drink a glass of wine or beer once or twice a month socially, so I haven't recently stopped heavy drinking.
No, I don't use asthma inhalers, thyroid medications, lithium, antidepressants, or antipsychotic drugs.
No one in my family has ever had hand tremors, Parkinson's disease, or nervous system disorders.
No, I have never had yellow eyes, jaundice, or any liver problems.
My periods used to be very regular, but over the past two months they have become very light and irregular.
My neck feels slightly full in the front, but it does not hurt to touch or when I swallow.
My eyes have felt a bit dry and irritated lately, but I haven't had double vision or noticed them bulging out.
No, I have not had any fever or chills.
I honestly thought I was developing severe anxiety or having panic attacks because of the constant heart racing.
I'm terrified that this rapid heartbeat is going to cause a heart attack or permanent heart damage.
I really hope you can prescribe something today to calm my heart down and stop this shaking.
I only have seasonal allergic rhinitis, which flares up occasionally in the spring.
I have never had any surgeries and I have never been hospitalized.
I only take an over-the-counter antihistamine once in a while when my allergies act up.
I don't have any allergies to medications that I know of.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any nicotine products.
I only have an occasional drink once or twice a month at social gatherings.
I work as a web designer and I live alone in an apartment.
My mother has an overactive thyroid condition, but my parents are otherwise healthy.
My last menstrual period started about two weeks ago, and the bleeding was unusually light.
My partner and I use condoms for birth control, and a home pregnancy test last week was negative.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 134/74 mmHg, pulse 108 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, temperature 37.2°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, anxious-appearing young female who appears restless and fidgety, with visible fine hand tremors.
Mild bilateral upper eyelid retraction and infrequent blinking; extraocular movements intact without proptosis or diplopia.
Symmetrically, diffusely enlarged thyroid gland, soft and non-tender without palpable nodules; faint vascular bruit audible.
Tachycardic rate with regular rhythm, crisp S1 and S2, and no murmurs, gallops, or rubs.
Skin is noticeably warm, smooth, and moist with mild palmar erythema; no pretibial edema or plaques.
Prominent high-frequency, fine postural tremor in both hands when arms are held outstretched; minimal resting tremor on lap.
Normal muscle tone throughout without cogwheel rigidity; finger tapping is rapid and brisk without decrement.
Finger-to-nose test shows intact targeting without dysmetria or intention tremor; gait is steady with normal stride and arm swing.
Brisk symmetric deep tendon reflexes (3+) at the biceps and knees with rapid relaxation phase; plantar responses flexor.
